title: Quantitative imaging-pathology correlation in nodular fasciitis and diagnostic discrimination from sarcoma.
abstract: Objectives To investigate associations between key magnetic resonance imaging features of nodular fasciitis (NF) and quantitative histopathologic biomarkers, and to evaluate whether their integration provides complementary information for differentiating NF from soft tissue sarcoma (STS) in diagnostically equivocal settings. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 128 patients with NF and 133 with STS who underwent preoperative 3-T MRI between May 2023 and June 2025. Two blinded musculoskeletal radiologists independently evaluated predefined imaging features, including fascial tail sign, T2 heterogeneity score, enhancement pattern, perilesional edema, and mean/minimum apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). Histopathology quantified cellular density, collagen content, and myxoid degeneration. Imaging-pathology correlations were assessed using Spearman analysis and multivariable regression. Diagnostic performance of MRI-only, pathology-only, and combined models was evaluated using logistic regression, receiver operating characteristic (ROC), area under the curve (AUC) analysis, calibration, decision curve analysis, and bootstrap validation. Results T2 heterogeneity correlated positively with myxoid degeneration (ρ = 0.52) and negatively with collagen content (ρ = -0.28) (p < 0.001). Mean ADC correlated inversely with cellular density (ρ = -0.63, p < 0.001). Mean ADC was significantly higher in NF than STS (p < 0.001). The combined model outperformed MRI alone (AUC, 0.96 vs 0.89) and demonstrated greater net clinical benefit. Bootstrap validation confirmed stable performance (mean AUC, 0.960; 95% confidence interval, 0.938-0.978). Conclusion Imaging features of NF were associated with underlying stromal and cellular substrates. Integrating imaging features with quantitative pathology biomarkers may support radiology-pathology concordance assessment in selected diagnostically equivocal cases. Key points Question How can we improve radiology-pathology concordance and reduce interpretative variability for NF cases presenting with suspicious, diagnostically equivocal magnetic resonance imaging findings? Findings T2 heterogeneity and diffusion measurements are associated with stromal composition and cellularity, while predefined MRI features demonstrated substantial-to-excellent inter-reader agreement. Critical relevance statement Embedding explicit AHA criteria in the prompt let an 8B model approach 671B-model agreement (38.91-81.52%), supporting standardized text-based workflows without fine-tuning.

title: MRI-based deep-learning radiomics nomogram for differentiating FIGO 2023 stage I from stage II-IV endometrial cancer: a multicenter study.
abstract: Objectives Preoperative identification of FIGO 2023 stage I endometrial cancer (EC) is important for treatment planning. We aimed to develop and validate a deep-learning radiomics nomogram (DLRN) based on multiparametric MRI to distinguish stage I EC from stage II-IV disease. Materials and methods This study retrospectively enrolled patients from three centers. Patients from Centers 1 and 2 were randomly split into a training set (n = 616), and an internal test set (n = 158), and Center 3 served as an external test set (n = 232). The DLRN integrated deep-learning features, intratumoral and peritumoral radiomics features, and clinical characteristics. The DLRN was compared with clinical, radiomics, and deep-learning models. Discrimination was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with AUCs compared using DeLong's test. Results A total of 1006 patients (mean age, 56.5 ± 9.7 years) were analyzed. In the internal test set, the DLRN achieved an AUC of 0.852, higher than the clinical (0.673; p = 0.001), original radiomics (0.765; p = 0.030), and combined radiomics (0.793; p = 0.050) models. In the external test set, the DLRN remained robust (AUC = 0.829) and outperformed the clinical, original radiomics, and combined radiomics models (AUC = 0.680, 0.681, and 0.743; all p < 0.005). With DLRN assistance, radiologists showed improved diagnostic performance. Conclusion The MRI-based DLRN showed robust discrimination between FIGO 2023 stage I and stage II-IV EC across test sets, supporting its potential for preoperative risk stratification and decision support. Key points Question The introduction of the FIGO 2023 staging system has made the differentiation between stages more challenging, highlighting the need for better tools. Findings A new MRI-based deep-learning radiomics nomogram (DLRN) accurately identifies high-risk patients, significantly outperforming traditional and individual clinical prediction methods. Critical relevance statement This tool helps doctors make better preoperative treatment plans, potentially improving patient outcomes in endometrial cancer.

title: Predatory publishing in radiology: advice for early-career researchers.
abstract: Predatory journals typically use practices based on deceit, misleading information, lack of transparency, and the absence of rigorous peer review. Within radiology, such journals frequently publish articles with minimal editorial oversight and limited scientific credibility. The relevance of this issue in radiology has grown as imaging research has expanded rapidly, particularly in artificial intelligence (AI), quantitative imaging, and subspecialty-driven innovation. Given the academic pressure created by the "publish or perish" culture, this environment makes early-career radiologists especially vulnerable to predatory journals that promise rapid publication and high acceptance rates. Predatory journals exploit this environment by sending unsolicited invitations to publish or join editorial boards, frequently using flattering language and promising unrealistic publication timelines. These journals generally lack robust peer review, methodological scrutiny, and transparency and are typically not indexed in established databases such as PubMed, Scopus, or Web of Science. Consequently, articles published in these outlets have reduced visibility, limited citation potential, and minimal impact on radiological science or clinical practice. Furthermore, publication in predatory journals may adversely affect academic reputation and career advancement, as hiring and funding committees increasingly prioritise journal quality and publication integrity. The rapid expansion of radiology research, particularly in diagnostic imaging, interventional radiology, and AI-powered applications, may increase opportunities for the dissemination of low-quality or insufficiently validated evidence through predatory journals. Raising awareness of predatory publishing practices and consistently applying evaluation tools such as the "Think. Check. Submit." framework, are fundamental to safeguarding scientific integrity and ensuring the dissemination of high-quality radiological research. KEY POINTS: Question Predatory publishing is a growing concern in radiology, driven by rising publication pressure and the "publish or perish" culture. Early-career researchers are particularly susceptible to unethical journals that offer rapid publication. Findings Predatory journals frequently bypass rigorous peer review, lack transparency, and are often not indexed in major databases. These journals exploit authors through unsolicited invitations and prioritise profit over scientific quality. Critical relevance statement Avoiding predatory journals is important for protecting research credibility, career progression, and scientific integrity. Publications in these outlets may disseminate unreliable evidence and are often disregarded in academic and clinical evaluations.

title: Multiphasic CT radiomics-clinical model for predicting acute pancreatitis recurrence: a multicenter survival analysis.
abstract: Objectives To develop and externally validate a predictive model integrating multiphasic CT radiomics and clinical variables to estimate recurrence risk after first-episode acute pancreatitis (AP). Materials and methods This multicenter retrospective study included 548 patients with first-episode AP (training, n = 272; internal validation, n = 117; external validation, n = 159). Clinical and multiphasic CT data were collected, with recurrence as the primary endpoint. After stability-based feature selection, clinical, radiomics, and combined Cox models were constructed. Performance was evaluated using the C-index and time-dependent AUC, with SHAP for interpretability. Results A total of 548 patients were included (median age 42 years; 363 men). Recurrence rates were similar across cohorts (30.1%, 29.9%, and 28.3%; p = 0.702). The combined model achieved C-indices of 0.783 and 0.775 in the internal and external validation cohorts, respectively, numerically higher than those of the clinical model (0.748 and 0.750) and radiomics model (0.647 and 0.619), although the incremental improvement over the clinical model was not statistically significant. In the external validation cohort, time-dependent AUCs remained acceptable through 36 months but declined at 48 months. High-risk patients had lower 3-year recurrence-free survival than low-risk patients (37.4% vs 86.8%; log-rank p < 0.001). SHAP analysis identified the NC-3mm-Radscore as the most influential imaging-derived variable, whereas etiology-targeted prevention was the dominant protective factor. Conclusions The combined model demonstrated acceptable discrimination for predicting recurrence within the first 24 months after first-episode AP and may facilitate individualized follow-up and secondary prevention strategies. Key points Question Can a multiphasic CT radiomics-clinical model improve prediction of AP recurrence over clinical factors alone in a multicenter setting? Findings The combined model demonstrated numerically higher predictive performance than the clinical model, though the incremental improvement was not statistically significant. Critical relevance statement This study critically evaluates the added value of multiphasic radiomics for recurrence prediction in AP, demonstrating that while radiomics captures baseline microenvironmental vulnerability, post-discharge clinical interventions remain the dominant dynamic drivers.

title: AI-accelerated compressed sensing and deep learning reconstruction for colon MRI: prospective validation of image quality and preliminary assessment of staging accuracy versus contrast-enhanced CT.
abstract: Objectives To prospectively validate an AI-accelerated MRI protocol combining L₁-regularized compressed sensing and deep learning reconstruction for colon cancer staging, compared with contrast-enhanced CT (CECT). Materials and methods This single-center study (August 2022-April 2024) enrolled 132 patients with pathologically confirmed colon cancer who underwent both 3.0-T non-contrast MRI and CECT within 1 week. Patients unable to complete an MRI were excluded. MRI sequences included T1- and T2-weighted imaging and diffusion-weighted imaging. Image quality was assessed using a 4-point Likert scale, alongside quantitative analysis of contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) and edge rise distance (ERD). Surgical pathology correlation was available for 33 cases. Five radiologists independently reviewed the images. Results Among 153 matched examination pairs from 132 patients (mean age, 58 ± 11 years), AI-MRI outperformed CECT in both qualitative and quantitative measures. MRI yielded higher image quality scores (4 [IQR 3-4] vs. 3 [IQR 3-3]), improved CNR (5.5 [IQR 4.2-7.0] vs. 1.3 [IQR 0.7-2.2]), and reduced ERD (1.6 mm [IQR 1.2-2.8] vs. 3.7 mm [IQR 2.8-5.0]). MRI provided superior peritoneal sharpness (75.8%) and colonic wall visualization (100%), and superior or equivalent tumor conspicuity (92.2%) and nodal assessment (86.9%), whereas CECT demonstrated better artifact control (45.1%). In preliminary analyses, MRI achieved higher T-staging accuracy (78.8% vs. 30.3%) and N-staging specificity (93.3% vs. 13.3%). Conclusion The AI-accelerated MRI protocol significantly outperformed CECT in image quality and preliminary staging accuracy for colon cancer evaluation while eliminating radiation exposure. Key points Question Can an AI-accelerated MRI protocol provide superior image quality and staging performance compared with contrast-enhanced CT, which has limited diagnostic accuracy for colon cancer staging? Findings AI-accelerated MRI using L₁-regularized compressed sensing and deep learning reconstruction achieved superior image quality and higher preliminary staging accuracy than contrast-enhanced CT. Critical Relevance Statement AI-accelerated MRI improves image quality and staging confidence without radiation exposure, supporting its potential to enhance preoperative assessment and clinical decision-making in colon cancer.

title: Deep learning-based detection and classification of airway nodules on CT for early medical intervention.
abstract: Objectives Airway lesions are common CT findings in interval and post-screen lung cancers; however, airway nodules are frequently overlooked. Robust artificial intelligence (AI) tools for characterizing airway nodules remain limited. This study aimed to develop and evaluate deep learning-based models for the detection and classification of airway nodules on low-dose CT(LDCT) as a second-reading tool. Materials and methods 1813 segmental and more proximal airway nodules were retrospectively identified from 1107 LDCT of 1043 participants. A sphere-based center-points matching network, first used to establish a lung nodule detection model, was transferred to airway nodules and enhanced by incorporating coordinate and multiscale attention. The model was trained on 907 proximal airway nodules and independently tested on 738 proximal nodules across four hospitals. The clinical utility of the AI tool was evaluated through human-AI interaction. For nodule classification, a 3D SEResNeXt101-based model was trained, validated and tested using 286 airway nodules (121 benign, 165 malignant) with a 6:2:2 split and evaluated in an independent testing dataset. Results On the independent testing set, the detection model achieved a high sensitivity of 73.7%. Human-AI interaction demonstrated AI assistance significantly improved radiologists' performance, increasing sensitivity from 39.5% to 72.9% and F1-score from 49.4% to 77.2%, while reducing diagnosis time from 83.8 s to 61.8 s. The classification model showed high sensitivities of 82.1%, 71.4%, 94.3%, 72.7% and specificities of 62.7%, 73.9%, 73.9%, 87.5% across multicenter training, validation, testing and independent testing sets, respectively. Conclusion This AI system significantly enhances the detection and classification of proximal airway nodules, guiding early medical intervention. Key points Question Improved early detection and classification of airway nodules are critical for lung cancer mortality reduction, but AI-based CAD systems targeting airway nodules remain scarce. Findings The DL models for detection and classification of proximal airway nodules on chest CT were developed and assisted radiologists to achieve higher detection accuracy. Critical Relevance Statement The clinical applications of the proposed DL-based system for detecting and classifying proximal airway nodules on chest CT scans help radiologists reduce missed/delayed diagnoses and shorten diagnostic time as a second-reading tool, guiding medical intervention and improving clinical outcomes.

Human-AI interaction demonstrated AI assistance significantly improved radiologists' performance, increasing sensitivity from 39.5% to 72.9% and F1-score from 49.4% to 77.2%, while reducing diagnosis time from 83.8 s to 61.8 s. The classification model showed high sensitivities of 82.1%, 71.4%, 94.3%, 72.7% and specificities of 62.7%, 73.9%, 73.9%, 87.5% across multicenter training, validation, testing and independent testing sets, respectively.

Conclusion

This AI system significantly enhances the detection and classification of proximal airway nodules, guiding early medical intervention.

Key points

Question Improved early detection and classification of airway nodules are critical for lung cancer mortality reduction, but AI-based CAD systems targeting airway nodules remain scarce. Findings The DL models for detection and classification of proximal airway nodules on chest CT were developed and assisted radiologists to achieve higher detection accuracy. Critical Relevance Statement The clinical applications of the proposed DL-based system for detecting and classifying proximal airway nodules on chest CT scans help radiologists reduce missed/delayed diagnoses and shorten diagnostic time as a second-reading tool, guiding medical intervention and improving clinical outcomes.

title: Deep learning-based quantification of CT changes after 1 year of pirfenidone treatment as a prognostic marker in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the prognostic value of changes in deep learning-based CT quantification following 1 year of pirfenidone treatment in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Materials and methods This study included patients with IPF who received at least 1 year of pirfenidone between September 2009 and March 2022 at two hospitals. The extent of normal lung and fibrosis (sum of reticular opacity and honeycombing) was quantified on baseline and 1-year follow-up chest CT scans using a deep learning-based tool, and the changes were calculated. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality or lung transplantation; the secondary outcome was a ≥ 10% absolute decline in forced vital capacity (FVC) occurring after the 1-year follow-up. Associations between changes in CT quantification and these outcomes were assessed using Cox proportional hazards regression analyses. Results A total of 436 patients (341 men; mean age, 69.8 years) were included. Greater preservation of normal lung extent over 1 year was associated with a lower risk of the composite outcome (adjusted hazard ratio (HR) per 5% increase: 0.90; 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.85, 0.96; p < 0.001), whereas increases in fibrosis extent were associated with a higher risk (adjusted HR per 5% increase: 1.16, 95% CI: 1.06, 1.27, p = 0.002). Regarding the secondary outcome of ≥ 10% absolute FVC decline, only the change in fibrosis extent remained a significant predictor (adjusted HR per 5% increase: 1.26, 95% CI: 1.09, 1.45, p = 0.001). Conclusions Changes in deep learning-based CT quantification results over 1 year of pirfenidone treatment demonstrated significant prognostic value in patients with IPF. Key points Question Disease progression and mortality in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) continue to occur unpredictably beyond 1 year of pirfenidone treatment. Findings Changes in deep learning-based quantification of normal lung and fibrosis extent after 1 year of pirfenidone treatment were significant prognostic predictors. Critical relevance statement Incorporating 1-year changes in deep learning-based CT quantification improves prognostication of mortality, lung transplantation, and lung function decline, supporting more individualized risk stratification in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

title: Advancing placenta accreta spectrum diagnosis: is 3-T MRI or combined MRI with ultrasound the answer?
abstract: Objective This study compares the diagnostic performance of US and 3-T MRIin diagnosing placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) disorder using final histopathological and surgical findings and explores the benefit of using a combined MRI and US approach to diagnose PAS. Materials and methods We retrospectively reviewed electronic medical records of all patients undergoing 3-T MRIplacenta at our institution between January 2020 and November 2023. The gold standard for PAS outcome was histopathology, and where unavailable, we referred to the operative notes. Patients without surgical or histopathologic data, and non-diagnostic MRI studies were excluded. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), confidence intervals, and p-values were generated for MRI, US, and combined MRI + US to detect PAS with subgroup analysis for placenta accreta/increta and percreta. Results Eighty-eight patients met the inclusion criteria. The sensitivity and specificity of MRI for all PAS was 100.0% and 80.0% (p < 0.001), compared to US 89.5% and 62.0% (p < 0.001), and combined MRI + US 100.0% and 56.0% (p < 0.001), respectively. For diagnosing placenta percreta, MRI had a sensitivity and specificity of 83.3% and 94.3% (p < 0.001), compared to US 55.6% and 94.3% (p < 0.001) and combined MRI + US 83.3% and 92.9% (p < 0.001). Conclusion Both US and 3-T MRIdemonstrated strong diagnostic performances for detecting PAS, with 3-T MRIdemonstrating stronger performance in this selective cohort, and not further improved by including US data. The continued use of US, MRI and clinical data for evaluating PAS disorder treatment options is recommended. Key points Question No dedicated study has evaluated the diagnostic performance of 3-T MRIor the combined use of MRI with US in PAS. Findings 3-T MRIdemonstrates high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing PAS. The combined MRI and US assessment does not further improve diagnostic performance for PAS. Critical relevance statement 3-T MRImay be particularly useful as an adjunct in selected high-risk patients, equivocal ultrasound cases, or cases requiring assessment of myoinvasive disease and multidisciplinary surgical planning.

title: Impact of lung cancer screening on the workload of radiology professionals.
abstract: Objectives Lung cancer screening (LCS) with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) significantly reduces mortality among high-risk individuals, yet implementation remains limited at national and European levels. The Strengthening the Screening of Lung Cancer (SOLACE) Project aims to facilitate the implementation of equitable LCS. While considering the overall impact of LCS, we identified a lack of systematic evaluation on the impact on the workload of radiology professionals, including radiologists and radiographers. This multicentric, European-wide study prospectively examines the effects of LCS on radiology healthcare workers. Materials and methods A survey-based cross-sectional study was conducted among European radiology professionals engaged in LCS to evaluate their experiences across seven domains: impacts on workload, workflow specifics, reporting practices, artificial intelligence (AI) use, participation in training programmes, potential professional development, and overall support for LCS. Results We evaluated 56 responses (mean age 46 ± 10.8 years; 27 men) from 14 countries. About half of respondents (53.6%; n = 30) reported increased working hours, but only 21.6% (n = 11) felt overworked due to LCS. No significant factors were directly associated with feeling overworked. Most respondents (86.7%; n = 39) perceived increased expertise in assessing LCS LDCTs throughout screening, and 91.1% (n = 51) expressed support for the implementation of LCS. Conclusion Although LCS increased workload for many radiology professionals, few reported feeling overworked. Despite the added demands, there may be added benefits for radiology professionals. Taken together, these findings emphasise the importance of continuously evaluating and monitoring how LCS affects the workload of radiology healthcare professionals. Key points Question As wider implementation of lung cancer screening occurs in Europe, it is critical to consider its impact on radiology professionals' workload and associated workforce demands. Findings Although lung cancer screening increased workload for many radiology professionals, few felt overworked, and the majority perceived increased diagnostic confidence and support for screening implementation. Critical relevance statement Lung cancer screening via LDCT plays a critical role in detecting cancer earlier and improving survival. With growing support for the broader implementation of LCS, it is essential to consider its potential impact on the workload of radiology professionals.

title: Enhanced prognosis stratification following surgery for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma to optimize clinical decisions by reflecting tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment.
abstract: Objective Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has an extremely dismal postoperative prognosis. Conventional TNM staging cannot adequately characterize tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment, leading to suboptimal risk stratification. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an integrated prognostic system for PDAC by combining deep learning (DL)-based radiomic features with guideline‑recommended clinicopathological variables. Materials and methods This multicenter retrospective study included 592 patients with PDAC who underwent R0 surgical resection. A Swin Transformer-assisted DL classifier (Outcome Prediction for PDAC, OP-PDAC) was built using multi-planar contrast-enhanced CT scans (axial, coronal, and sagittal planes). Radiogenomic analysis was conducted in 41 patients to elucidate the biological underpinnings of the OP-PDAC. Furthermore, the Intelligent Prognosis Stratification System (IPSS-PDAC) was developed by incorporating clinicopathological variables into the OP-PDAC framework. Results In the derivation and test cohorts, the C‑index of OP-PDAC for predicting 1‑year disease‑free survival (DFS) ranged from 0.807 to 0.844, which was significantly higher than that of the clinicopathological model (CP-PDAC; C‑index, 0.631-0.656). The IPSS-PDAC further enhanced predictive performance, yielding a C‑index of 0.836-0.871, and enabled effective stratification for both DFS and overall survival (all log‑rank p < 0.01). Radiogenomic analysis revealed that high‑risk patients exhibited an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, elevated stromal scores, activated oncogenic pathways, and reduced CD8 + T‑cell infiltration. Conclusion IPSS-PDAC is a non-invasive and robust prognostic stratification system that integrates imaging features and clinicopathological features. By sensitively reflecting tumor heterogeneity and TME, it provides references for clinical decision-making in the postoperative management of PDAC patients. Key points Question This study constructs an integrated prognostic model combining imaging signatures and guideline-recommended clinicopathological variables to address unmet clinical challenges in postoperative risk stratification for PDAC patients. Findings A multi-planar Swin Transformer-based deep learning model (IPSS-PDAC) achieves a C-index of 0.836-0.871 for disease-free survival prediction. Critical relevance statement High-risk patients stratified by the OP-PDAC model display a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, activation of core oncogenic signaling pathways, and reduced CD8 + T-cell infiltration.

Question This study constructs an integrated prognostic model combining imaging signatures and guideline-recommended clinicopathological variables to address unmet clinical challenges in postoperative risk stratification for PDAC patients. Findings A multi-planar Swin Transformer-based deep learning model (IPSS-PDAC) achieves a C-index of 0.836-0.871 for disease-free survival prediction. Critical relevance statement High-risk patients stratified by the OP-PDAC model display a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, activation of core oncogenic signaling pathways, and reduced CD8+ T-cell infiltration.

title: Prostate: simplified MRI anatomy recognition and training-the P-SMART study: a novel approach to defining prostatic apex, mid-gland and base.
abstract: Objectives Precise lesion localisation on prostate MRI-specifically, identification of whether at the apex, mid-gland, or base-is essential for effective communication and clinical management. This study aimed to assess interobserver agreement of current practice using the Prostate Imaging-Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) against a novel anatomy-based approach, P-SMART (Prostate Simplified MRI Anatomy Recognition and Training). Materials and methods This multi-reader, two-phase agreement study, used axial and sagittal T2-weighted MRI from a publicly available dataset. Forty MRI cases were annotated with four regions of interest (ROIs). Readers were asked to document ROI location-apex, mid-gland, or base-first using the PI-RADS method, then following a 3-week washout period and short educational intervention, using the P-SMART method. Interobserver agreement was evaluated using Fleiss' kappa (κ) statistics and compared following bootstrap resampling using a paired t-test. Subgroup analyses were performed by reader expertise and prostate size. Results Following quality assurance, 156 ROIs were evaluated by 43 readers in each phase of the study. Overall interobserver agreement improved with P-SMART vs PI-RADS (κ = 0.571 vs 0.399; p < 0.001). In subgroup analyses, improvements were consistent for experts (0.663 vs 0.435; p < 0.001), non-experts (0.530 vs 0.393; p < 0.001), large prostates (0.518 vs 0.325; p < 0.001), and small prostates (0.620 vs 0.461; p < 0.001). Conclusion The P-SMART approach, designed to align with the PI-RADS sector map, yielded significantly higher interobserver agreement for prostate lesion-level localisation than the PI-RADS method, across reader experience and gland size, though overall agreement was only moderate. Improved reproducibility may support biopsy targeting, active surveillance monitoring, and treatment planning. Key points Question Can a novel method of dividing the prostate into apex, mid-gland, and base improve reader agreement compared to current practice? Findings The P-SMART method to divide the prostate outperformed PI-RADS (Fleiss' kappa 0.571 vs 0.399), improving consistency across experience levels and prostate sizes. Relevance statement More reproducible prostate level assignment supports accurate lesion localisation for biopsy planning, active surveillance, and treatment planning. If validated, P-SMART may improve communication and could be integrated into reporting workflows and software tools.

title: Diagnostic performance benchmarks of MRI for prostate cancer: a large-scale cohort study of 33,759 patients.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the real-world diagnostic performance of PI-RADS for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) across large-scale worldwide cohorts. Materials and methods This multicenter observational study included 20,429 patients from nine Chinese institutions and a published worldwide meta-analysis dataset comprising 13,330 patients for comparison. All PI-RADS assessments were extracted from original MRI reports produced by clinical radiologists as part of standard diagnostic workflows. Summary receiver operating characteristic curves were constructed using a bivariate random-effects model, and center-level areas under the curve (AUCs) were pooled via random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup analyses were conducted. Results PI-RADS exhibited overall discriminatory performance for csPCa across nine Chinese cohorts comparable to the META results from 70 studies, though significant inter-center variation was observed. Using a PI-RADS ≥ 3 threshold, pooled sensitivity was 92.6% and specificity was 51.5%. At a PI-RADS ≥ 4 threshold, pooled specificity improved to 78.1%, with a sensitivity of 81.5%. The overall diagnostic performance was consistent across thresholds: The summary ROC (SROC) AUC was 0.903 for PI-RADS ≥ 3 and 0.826 for PI-RADS ≥ 4 in detecting csPCa at the meta-analysis level. Subgroup analyses indicated better performance among older patients (≥ 70 years) and those with higher PSA levels (> 20 ng/mL). PI-RADS v2.1 outperformed v2 or earlier versions in most clinical scenarios. Conclusions This large-scale real-world study provides critical multicenter evidence supporting the use of PI-RADS in clinical practice worldwide, while also revealing substantial variability in scoring and diagnostic performance across institutions. The findings offer an evidence-based overview of PI-RADS implementation in China and worldwide, highlighting both its utility and inconsistencies. Key points Question What are the real-world PI-RADS diagnostic performance benchmarks for clinically significant prostate cancer detection across diverse Chinese multicenter institutions versus global data? Findings PI-RADS demonstrated good overall performance (SROC AUC 0.903 at a threshold of ≥ 3), with superior discriminatory ability in older patients, higher PSA levels, and v2.1 users. Critical relevance statement This article critically assesses substantial inter-institutional heterogeneity in PI-RADS performance, highlighting that pooled estimates should not replace local calibration and that regionally adapted implementation strategies are essential for advancing clinical radiology practice.

title: Feasibility of one-stop multi-energy dynamic photon-counting perfusion CT for resectable HCC evaluation: lesion detection and histopathological correlations.
abstract: Objectives To assess the feasibility of one-stop multi-energy dynamic volume perfusion photon-counting CT (VP-PCCT) for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) evaluation, including lesion detection and correlations with histopathology. Materials and methods From July 2024 to June 2025, 407 participants with suspected malignant liver lesions prospectively underwent VP-PCCT, and 177 patients with pathology-confirmed HCC who received three-phase energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT) were retrospectively enrolled for comparisons of image quality and lesion detectability. Single-phase images reconstructed from VP-PCCT perfusion datasets were compared with EID-CT. Perfusion parameters were analyzed between groups stratified separately by histological grade and microvascular invasion (MVI), and logistic regression was employed to identify independent indicators. Results Ninety-two participants [median age, 62 years (IQR, 53-69); 76 males] with pathology-confirmed HCC were included in the VP-PCCT group and matched with 92 in the EID-CT group. Compared with EID-CT, 40-keV VP-PCCT provided comparable image quality for HCC and vessels with a similar tumor detection rate but a lower radiation dose. Poorly-differentiated HCCs showed higher tumor hepatic perfusion index (HPI tumor ) and peritumoral blood flow (BF peritumor ); MVI-positive HCCs exhibited lower tumor arterial liver perfusion (ALP tumor ) and normalized blood flow of peritumoral region (BF norm_peritumor ) (all p < 0.05). HPI tumor [odds ratio (OR): 1.06] and BF peritumor (OR: 1.04) were independent risk factors for poorly differentiated HCC, whereas decreased ALP tumor (OR: 0.97) and BF norm_peritumor (OR: 0.25) were associated with MVI positivity (all p < 0.05). Conclusions One-stop VP-PCCT delivers high-quality morphologic and perfusion evaluation in a single low-dose scan, with hemodynamic profiles that may be associated with histological grade and MVI status. Key points Question Clinical use of dynamic volume perfusion CT for comprehensively evaluating HCC without additional multiphase contrast-enhanced imaging remains limited. Findings Multi-energy dynamic photon-counting perfusion CT provided high-quality morphologic imaging of HCC at a low dose, with perfusion parameters independently indicating poorly differentiated HCC and MVI. Critical relevance statement One-stop multi-energy dynamic photon-counting perfusion CT enables high-quality morphologic and functional assessment in a single low-dose scan, providing comprehensive HCC evaluation with hemodynamic profiling that may support the assessment of histological grade and MVI.

title: Radiomics analysis of brain-tumor interface on multiparametric MRI for prediction of brain metastasis primary site.
abstract: Objectives Brain metastasis (BM) frequently occurs in advanced cancer patients, and accurate identification of the primary origin is essential for personalized treatment. Conventional imaging often lacks sensitivity and specificity for BM source prediction. This study aimed to develop and validate a multiparametric MRI-based radiomics model emphasizing brain-tumor interface (BTI) features to improve noninvasive BM origin identification. Materials and methods The primary cohort included 429 patients (740 BMs) from two centers, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), small cell lung cancer (SCLC), breast cancer (BC), and gastrointestinal cancer (GIC), and an independent validation cohort of 33 patients (84 BMs) from a third center. All underwent pre-treatment 3.0 T MRI with T1-weighted contrast-enhanced (T1CE) and T2-weighted (T2W) sequences. Radiomic features were extracted from tumor core and BTI regions (2, 4, 6, 8 mm). Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used for feature selection, and radiomics signatures (RS) were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Results The constructed RS-BTI4 based on the 4-mm BTI region generated the best overall performance, with area under the ROC curve (AUCs) in the training cohort were 0.855 (LC/NLC), 0.910 (SCLC/NSCLC), and 0.890 (BC/GIC); in validation cohort, 0.726, 0.856, and 0.809; and in external validation cohort, 0.739, 0.750, and 0.792, respectively. RS-BTI4 consistently outperformed models based on other BTI radial widths and the whole tumor region in identifying the primary origin of BM. Conclusion BTI-derived radiomic features demonstrate strong potential for noninvasive identification of BM origin, with the 4-mm BTI region showing optimal predictive performance. Key points Question Conventional MRI cannot reliably identify the primary origin of brain metastases, particularly when the primary tumor remains unknown at diagnosis. Findings The 4-mm brain-tumor interface model showed the most favorable overall performance, measured by area under the curve, across three binary classification tasks and validation cohorts. Critical relevance statement Integrating brain-tumor interface radiomics with multiparametric MRI may improve noninvasive estimation of BM origin and support more targeted diagnostic evaluation in clinical radiology.

title: Peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations in the 2025 ISSVA classification: a practical MRI approach.
abstract: The 2025 update of the International Society for the Study of Vascular Anomalies (ISSVA) classification introduced several imaging-relevant changes, including the recognition of potentially unique vascular anomalies. Although the main framework for vascular tumors remains unchanged, with continued subdivision into benign, borderline, and malignant tumors, the most radiologically relevant structural changes concern vascular malformations, which were reorganized into fast-flow lesions, slow-flow lesions, and developmental anomalies of named vessels. These updates are important for radiologists because imaging plays a central role in assessing hemodynamic characteristics, defining lesion extent, and identifying findings relevant to procedural planning and multidisciplinary management. This educational review presents an author-derived four-step framework that organizes established MRI observations for peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations according to the structure and terminology of the 2025 ISSVA classification, including hemodynamic assessment, vascular components, tissue composition, lesion extent, and treatment-relevant anatomy. KEY POINTS: Question Imaging-relevant organizational and terminology changes in the 2025 ISSVA classification require practical guidance for consistent MRI assessment and reporting of peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations. Findings An author-derived four-step, flow-based framework organizes hemodynamics, dominant vascular components, tissue composition, lesion extent, and treatment-relevant anatomy into structured MRI assessment. title: Etoposide-induced angina in a patient with small cell lung carcinoma: a case report.
abstract: Background The combination of cisplatin and etoposide is a standard therapy for small cell lung cancer; however, ischemic heart disease is a known complication. We report a rare case of effort angina pectoris that worsened during initial treatment of small cell lung cancer with etoposide. Case presentation A 73-year-old Asian male was admitted to our hospital with effort angina. Coronary angiography revealed severe stenosis with significant calcification of the proximal right coronary artery. Computed tomography revealed a 21-mm-sized nodule in the right upper lobe and hilar lymphadenopathy suggestive of lung cancer. The patient underwent thoracoscopic wedge resection before coronary revascularization, and intraoperative findings indicated a small cell carcinoma with hilar lymph node metastases. Early postoperative definitive treatment consisting of chemotherapy with cisplatin plus etoposide and accelerated hyperfractionated radiation was planned. During the first chemotherapy session, on postoperative day 7, the patient complained of chest pain, and an electrocardiogram showed slight ST depression in leads V5 and V6 while receiving etoposide; nitroglycerin improved his symptoms. Although treatment was resumed with the administration of nicorandil the next day, the same symptoms were observed during the infusion of etoposide. Accordingly, chemoradiation therapy was suspended and revascularization of the right coronary artery was performed. Etoposide and cisplatin were readministered 3 days after revascularization, without any chest symptoms. Conclusion Chemotherapy for malignant tumors carries the risk of progression to coronary artery disease. To prevent serious ischemic events, sufficient discussions between oncologists and cardiologists and careful observation of chest symptoms are needed.

title: Very late local recurrence of chromophobe renal cell carcinoma 15 years after nephrectomy: a case report.
abstract: Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (chRCC) is a rare subtype of renal cell carcinoma, accounting for approximately 5% of cases. Although generally associated with a favorable prognosis, late recurrences may occur. Local recurrence more than a decade after nephrectomy is exceptionally rare, and optimal management remains poorly defined. We report a 79-year-old Greek man who underwent radical left nephrectomy and adrenalectomy in 2009 for a 13 × 10 × 9 cm moderately differentiated chRCC, classified in the original pathology report as pT2 pNX pMX, G2, R0. Fifteen years later, he presented with progressive limitation of left hip flexion and increasing constipation. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a solitary 9 × 8 × 7.5 cm left para-aortic retroperitoneal mass without radiologically detectable distant metastatic disease. Biopsy findings were consistent with recurrent renal cell carcinoma. The lesion was clinically classified as a local recurrence based on its location within the previous nephrectomy operative field and the absence of other metastatic lesions, although a solitary metastasis could not be unequivocally excluded histopathologically. After multidisciplinary assessment, complete surgical resection with systematic retroperitoneal lymph-node dissection was performed. Histopathological examination showed morphological features compatible with recurrence or metastasis of the previous chRCC, tumor-free margins, tumor-free sampled peritumoral skeletal muscle, and 0/16 involved lymph nodes. Immunohistochemical analysis was not performed. At 1-year follow-up, the patient remained clinically well with no radiological evidence of local recurrence or distant metastatic disease. Very late recurrence of chRCC may occur after a prolonged disease-free interval. In carefully selected patients with isolated and potentially resectable recurrence, complete surgical resection may represent a feasible treatment option within an individualized multidisciplinary approach. The 1-year follow-up in this case is insufficient to establish long-term oncological control, and continued surveillance is warranted.

title: Cell-free DNA-guided detection, surveillance, and therapeutic adaptation for breast cancer.
abstract: Plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) analysis provides a minimally invasive approach to breast cancer assessment across early detection, minimal residual disease (MRD) monitoring, and treatment adaptation in advanced disease. This review evaluates these applications by distinguishing analytical validity, clinical detection performance, prognostic validity, and clinical utility. In early detection, assays integrating genomic, epigenomic, fragmentomic, and protein-based features have shown encouraging performance in evaluated cohorts; however, sensitivity remains limited in low-burden disease, particularly stage I breast cancer. Their potential clinical role depends on the incremental information they provide beyond established imaging and diagnostic pathways. In the curative-intent setting, circulating tumor DNA detection after treatment is associated with recurrence risk and can precede clinical or radiographic relapse, supporting prognostic stratification and the design of MRD-guided intervention trials. Whether such interventions improve clinical outcomes remains a central unresolved question. In advanced breast cancer, plasma genotyping supports treatment selection in defined molecular contexts. Randomized trials of ESR1 mutation-guided endocrine switching have demonstrated progression-free survival benefits with specific treatment strategies, providing evidence beyond biomarker-outcome associations, although overall survival benefit remains to be established. Across applications, interpretation depends on assay characteristics, molecular input, disease setting, sampling schedule, and the clinical decision being evaluated. Future studies should connect assay performance to patient benefit through comparison with existing care, clinically meaningful endpoints, and assessment of treatment burden and downstream investigations. This approach will help define where cfDNA testing can contribute meaningfully to breast cancer management.

title: Deep learning denoising and deep learning-augmented contrast enhancement improve ultra-high-resolution photon-counting-detector CCTA image quality.
abstract: Objective Ultrahigh-resolution (UHR) coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) using a photon-counting detector (PCD) provides excellent spatial resolution but is limited by increased image noise. We evaluated whether deep learning (DL)-based denoising and contrast enhancement can further improve UHR-CCTA image quality. Materials and methods UHR-CCTA scans from 25 patients with coronary artery disease were retrospectively analyzed. Images were reconstructed at 0.2-mm slice thickness without and with quantum iterative reconstruction (QIR, Q off -Q 4 ), and subsequently processed using a DL tool for denoising and increasing iodine contrast enhancement. Subjective image quality (sharpness, noise, vessel wall delineation, and overall quality) was assessed by three radiologists using a 5-point Likert scale. Objective analysis included signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and coronary wall sharpness. Differences between image sets were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results DL-based CCTA demonstrated significantly superior subjective image quality across all parameters compared to standard reconstructions, with an overall median image quality ([interquartile interval, IQR]: 4 [3-5] versus 2 [2-3], p < 0.001). SNR and CNR were significantly higher for DL-based CCTA across all QIR levels (all p < 0.001). The highest values were observed for DL-based CCTAQ 4 versus UHR-CCTAQ 4 (SNR: 258.0 ± 147.5 versus 145.2 ± 50.1; CNR: 25.8 ± 17.1 versus 11.1 ± 4.5; both p < 0.001). Coronary wall sharpness was improved for DL-based CCTA for Q 1-4 (all p < 0.027). Conclusion DL-based denoising and iodine contrast enhancement effectively reduce noise and improve anatomic detail in UHR-CCTA, providing incremental value beyond vendor-specific reconstruction, particularly at high QIR strength levels. Key points Question Deep learning reduces noise and enhances contrast in ultrahigh-resolution coronary CT angiography. Findings Image quality improves beyond standard iterative reconstruction methods, and vessel wall sharpness and diagnostic clarity significantly increase. Relevance statement This study aimed to determine at which levels of vendor-specific iterative reconstruction, DL-based denoising and contrast enhancement perform best in UHR CCTA, providing a foundation for future investigations on how these technical improvements may translate into diagnostic benefits.

title: Image quality and artefact reduction for tantalum clips in ocular proton therapy using photon-counting CT.
abstract: Objective Tantalum fiducials ("clips") used in intraocular proton therapy generate strong artefacts in conventional computed tomography, limiting the visibility of tumours and anatomical structures. This study investigated the potential of photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) for reducing tantalum-related artefacts. Materials and methods Two phantom models containing tantalum clips were examined using a photon-counting CT system and two conventional CT scanners with energy-integrating detectors (EICT). Reconstruction parameters, including tube voltage, image resolution, reconstruction kernel, virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI), and iterative metal artefact reduction (iMAR), were systematically optimised. Image quality was evaluated using objective metrics assessing homogeneity, noise, contrast, structural similarity, and artefact volume, complemented by a blinded subjective observer study. Correlations between objective and subjective results were analysed using Spearman's rank correlation. Results Objectively, PCCT showed no significant advantage over the modern EICT scanner but significantly outperformed the older-generation EICT therapy simulator. In contrast, blinded observers consistently preferred PCCT images. iMAR was the dominant factor influencing image quality. VMI alone did not yield relevant improvements. High-energy VMI (110 keV) combined with iMAR achieved the best subjective ratings. Higher spatial resolution due to smaller voxel sizes showed no clinically relevant benefit for artefact reduction. Soft reconstruction kernels provided the best balance between artefact suppression and image noise. Objective rankings correlated strongly with subjective assessments. Conclusion PCCT combined with iMAR improves subjective image quality in intraocular proton therapy and reduces the perceived severity of tantalum artefacts. Nevertheless, tantalum remains a major challenge in image-guided proton therapy, requiring further optimisation of imaging and reconstruction strategies. Key points Question Photon-counting CT may improve visualisation of tantalum clips and reduce metal artefacts in ocular proton therapy planning compared with conventional CT systems. Findings Photon-counting CT achieved the highest subjective image quality ratings, while iterative metal artefact reduction remained the dominant factor influencing artefact suppression. Relevance statement Photon-counting CT combined with iterative metal artefact reduction can improve visualisation of tantalum clips and surrounding anatomy in ocular proton therapy planning and may support more reliable tumour localisation despite limited objective differences compared with state-of-the-art conventional CT.

title: Time-dependent diffusion MRI in determining mismatch repair status of endometrial cancer.
abstract: Objectives Mismatch repair (MMR) proteins are important in determining therapeutic strategy in endometrial cancer (EC). We investigated the role of microstructural parameters derived from time-dependent diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (td-dMRI) in differentiating MMR status of EC. Materials and methods This prospective single-center study enrolled patients with suspected EC who underwent preoperative td-dMRI. Tumors were classified as MMR-deficient (dMMR) and MMR-proficient (pMMR) by immunohistochemistry. The microstructural parameters, including intracellular volume fraction ( vin ), cell diameter ( d ), cellularity ( ρ ), extracellular diffusivity ( Dex ), and water exchange rate constant ( kin ), were derived by fitting td-dMRI data with three methods (IMPULSED, JOINT, and EXCHANGE), together with the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). Differences in these microstructural parameters between dMMR and pMMR EC were compared. The diagnostic performances were evaluated by the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results Eighty-two patients (17 dMMR, 61.8 ± 10.1 years and 65 pMMR, 58.6 ± 11.8 years) were recruited. dMMR EC exhibited higher vin , ρ and lower Dex , ADC values than pMMR EC (p ≤ 0.003). IMPULSED and JOINT demonstrated higher AUCs than conventional ADC (p = 0.025 and 0.046, respectively). The combined selected microstructural parameters ( vin and Dex ) derived from JOINT achieved an AUC of 0.903; JOINT demonstrated superior parametric stability and marginally better calibration than IMPULSED. Conclusion In this exploratory study, td-dMRI discriminated between dMMR and pMMR ECs, providing information on the intricate microscopic organizational structures in tumors. The microstructural parameters may serve as a promising method to improve the diagnostic efficacy of diffusion-weighted MRI in differentiating MMR status of EC. Key points Question There remains an unmet need for noninvasive, preoperative tools to assess DNA MMR status in EC. Findings td-dMRI showed significant differences in microstructural parameters between dMMR and pMMR tumors. Relevance statement td-dMRI shows potential as a noninvasive imaging approach for preoperative assessment of MMR status in EC and may support individualized treatment planning.

The microstructural parameters may serve as a promising method to improve the diagnostic efficacy of diffusion-weighted MRI in differentiating MMR status of EC.

Key points

Question There remains an unmet need for noninvasive, preoperative tools to assess DNA MMR status in EC. Findings td-dMRI showed significant differences in microstructural parameters between dMMR and pMMR tumors. Relevance statement td-dMRI shows potential as a noninvasive imaging approach for preoperative assessment of MMR status in EC and may support individualized treatment planning.

title: Diagnostic accuracy and reliability of susceptibility map-weighted imaging in patients with clinically uncertain parkinsonian syndromes.
abstract: Objectives Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, accompanied by increased iron accumulation, particularly in the nigrosome-1 subregion. Differentiating neurodegenerative disorders like PD from non-neurodegenerative causes of parkinsonism can be challenging. In clinically uncertain parkinsonian syndrome (CUPS), dopamine transporter (DAT)-single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) can aid diagnosis. However, susceptibility map-weighted imaging (SMWI) provides a promising magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) alternative. We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and reliability of visual SMWI assessment by radiologists in CUPS and the added value of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven diagnostic software. Materials and methods Patients with CUPS who underwent DAT-SPECT between January 2019 and July 2023 were included. Four radiologists, blinded to clinical symptoms and diagnosis, visually rated nigrosome-1 on axial SMWI reconstructions as normal, unclear, or abnormal. After the initial assessment, the radiologists re-evaluated the scans with AI-driven software assistance, designed to classify and quantify nigrosome-1 integrity. The reference standard was the final clinical diagnosis incorporating DAT-SPECT results. Results One hundred eighty patients were included (mean age 67.9, range 31-86, 120 males), 84 with neurodegenerative and 96 with non-neurodegenerative parkinsonism. Mean diagnostic accuracy was 80% (range 73-83%), with substantial inter-rater reliability (Fleiss κ 0.65). With software assistance, diagnostic accuracy improved to 87% (range 85-91%), and inter-rater agreement increased to almost perfect (Fleiss κ 0.86). Conclusion SMWI, particularly with AI-driven software assistance, is a promising and accessible MRI-based technique that may support the diagnostic workup in clinically uncertain parkinsonism, aiding the distinction between neurodegenerative and non-neurodegenerative causes. Key points Question Can susceptibility map-weighted imaging (SMWI) reliably differentiate neurodegenerative from non-neurodegenerative parkinsonism in clinically uncertain cases, and does artificial intelligence (AI)-driven software assistance improve radiologist performance? Findings Visual assessment had an accuracy of 80%, with substantial inter-rater reliability. AI-driven software assistance increased accuracy to 87% and improved inter-rater reliability. Relevance statement SMWI can differentiate neurodegenerative from non-neurodegenerative parkinsonism in clinically uncertain cases and may support the diagnostic process by offering an accessible MRI-based technique, facilitating an efficient diagnostic workup, and enabling early diagnosis in clinically uncertain parkinsonism.

title: High-power radiofrequency ablation with optimized pulsing algorithm for renal tumors: initial clinical experience and safety profile.
abstract: Incidental diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma is increasing. While surgery remains the standard treatment for localized T1b or larger lesions, image-guided percutaneous ablation represents a valid alternative for T1a cases. Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is effective but limited by smaller ablation volumes and sensitivity to the heat-sink effect. Microwave ablation and cryoablation have emerged to address these limitations, although the first is susceptible to thermal injury to adjacent structures and the second requires multiple, larger probes and longer procedures. High-power RFA (HP-RFA) is a recent development that delivers higher energy (370 versus 200 W), enabling faster and larger ablations. This study evaluated the feasibility and safety of a novel HP-RFA system incorporating an impedance-controlled pulsed algorithm and internally cooled electrodes. Five patients with small renal tumors (mean diameter 2.3 cm) unsuitable for surgery underwent ultrasound- or computed tomography-guided HP-RFA. Technical success, safety, and early tumor control were assessed. All procedures were technically successful. No major complications occurred; one minor perirenal hematoma was managed conservatively. Follow-up imaging at 6 months demonstrated complete tumor ablation without local recurrence. These preliminary findings suggest that HP-RFA is feasible and safe for treating small renal tumors and may represent a promising evolution of RFA. Further studies are needed. KEY POINTS: Question Can HP-RFA provide feasible and safe minimally invasive treatment for small renal tumors while overcoming limitations of conventional RFA? Findings Technical success and efficacy of HP-RFA were achieved in 100% of cases. No major complications. Complete tumor ablation was accomplished. Relevance statement HP-RFA demonstrates feasibility, safety, and effective early tumor control in small renal tumors. By enabling larger, faster ablations, it may overcome limitations of conventional RFA and expand the employment of minimally invasive treatment options instead of surgical approaches.

title: MRI-based virtual radiographs of the pelvis for assessment of acetabular morphology.
abstract: Objectives We generated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based virtual radiographs (VRs) from hips with/without intra-articular contrast and compared them with conventional anteroposterior pelvic radiographs (CR) regarding measurement bias, interobserver and intraobserver agreement, and diagnosis of acetabular deformities; we also assessed hip deformity prevalence on VR in asymptomatic participants. Materials and methods Retrospective study of 50 patients (100 hips; mean age 34 years) with femoroacetabular impingement or hip dysplasia undergoing CR and unilateral magnetic resonance arthrography. Additionally, 53 asymptomatic participants underwent noncontrast MRI. Segmentation of the osseous pelvis was performed on T1-weighted volume interpolated breathhold examination (VIBE) Dixon MRI using 3D nnU-Net, pseudo-computed tomography generation, and cone-beam projection to generate VR. Acetabular coverage (lateral center edge angle (LCE), acetabular index (AI), anterior/posterior coverage, extrusion index (EI)), and acetabular version were compared between CR and VR. Interobserver agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and κ statistics; bias with Bland-Altman analysis. Results Interobserver agreement for VR ranged from moderate to almost perfect (ICC/κ 0.60-0.94), except for the AI. LCE showed no significant bias with ( - 0.2° ± 2.5, p = 0.663) or without contrast ( - 0.2° ± 2.2, p = 0.530). Systematic differences occurred for AI, EI, anterior/posterior coverage, and ischial spine sign; 57-75% of discrepancies were within CR interobserver variation. Diagnostic classification showed substantial agreement between CR and VR (κ = 0.62), comparable to CR interobserver agreement (κ = 0.70). In asymptomatic participants, 13% had acetabular dysplasia, 68% normal coverage, and 19% overcoverage. Conclusion MRI-based VR provides acetabular morphology assessment comparable to CR and enables radiation-free evaluation in symptomatic patients and asymptomatic populations. Key points Question Can MRI-based virtual radiographs reproduce conventional radiographic measurements of acetabular morphology, enabling radiation-free two-dimensional assessment in symptomatic patients and asymptomatic populations? Findings The lateral center-edge angle showed no significant bias between virtual and conventional radiographs; diagnostic classification of acetabular deformities agreed substantially (κ = 0.62), comparable to conventional radiograph interobserver agreement. Relevance Statement MRI-derived virtual radiographs can provide acetabular measurements comparable to conventional radiographs without ionizing radiation, supporting integration into three-dimensional surgical planning and enabling assessment in young patients and population-based cohorts where repeated radiographs are undesirable.

title: Oxygen-enhanced brain MRI using dynamic gradient-echo and MR fingerprinting.
abstract: Objectives Oxygen-enhanced brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) using dynamic three-dimensional (3D) gradient-echo and MR fingerprinting (MRF) was applied to evaluate oxygen transit from blood to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Materials and methods Twenty healthy participants, enrolled between December 2023 and March 2024, underwent 3-T MRI including Pre-oxygen inhalation 3D MRF (pre-O₂ MRF), dynamic 3D gradient-echo (volumetric interpolated breath-hold examination, VIBE) during oxygen inhalation, and post-oxygen inhalation 3D MRF (post-O₂ MRF). Pre-O₂ and post-O₂ MRF each consisted of two acquisitions. Signal intensity on dynamic VIBE and T1 relaxation times from MRF were evaluated in gray matter (GM), white matter (WM), surface CSF, and ventricles using volumes of interest (VOIs). Results Dynamic 3D VIBE demonstrated a rapid signal increase in surface CSF immediately after oxygen inhalation, with a smaller increase in GM. Post-oxygen inhalation VIBE signal was significantly higher than pre-oxygen inhalation signal in surface CSF (p < 0.001) and GM (p < 0.001). T1 relaxation times differed significantly across phases for GM, WM, and surface CSF (p < 0.001) as well as for ventricles (p = 0.024). Large effect sizes were observed for surface CSF (Cohen dz = 4.15) and GM (Cohen dz = 1.31) in dynamic 3D VIBE, as well as for surface CSF (Cohen f = 1.31) and GM (Cohen f = 0.73) in T1 relaxation time measurement, suggesting substantial physiological changes following oxygen inhalation. Conclusion Dynamic 3D VIBE images visualized oxygen inhalation-related signal change in the surface CSF, which were quantitatively validated by T1 relaxation time reductions derived from 3D MRF. Key points Question Can noninvasive oxygen-enhanced brain MRI visualize and quantify oxygen-related signal changes in cerebrospinal fluid using dynamic 3D gradient-echo and 3D MR fingerprinting? Findings Dynamic 3D gradient-echo showed rapid surface CSF signal increases after oxygen inhalation, accompanied by significant T1 reductions on 3D MR fingerprinting. Relevance statement This noninvasive oxygen-enhanced MR approach may provide a clinically feasible method for assessing oxygen transit into CSF and could support future investigations of human CSF dynamics. Dynamic 3D gradient-echo images visualized oxygen inhalation-related signal change in the surface CSF, which were quantitatively validated by T1 relaxation time reductions derived from 3D MRF.

title: MRI radiomics of pancreatic tumours: a systematic review of methodological quality and imaging reproducibility.
abstract: Objectives Radiomics holds potential for personalised treatment, but reproducibility is hindered by inconsistent reporting of imaging parameters and methodological details. This study aims to identify and evaluate key MR imaging parameters to support radiomics reproducibility and to systematically evaluate the quality of published MRI radiomics studies focused on pancreatic tumours. Materials and methods The literature search was conducted in the Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science databases. Human studies investigating MRI radiomics in pancreatic tumours were included. An imaging reporting checklist was developed and used to identify and evaluate imaging parameters in eligible studies. The methodological quality score (METRICS) and checklist for evaluation of radiomics research (CLEAR) score were calculated for each study. Results Seventy-eight studies, encompassing 241 MRI pulse sequences (143 anatomical and 98 functional), were included. The imaging checklist identified ten core items as key parameters for ensuring reproducible MRI radiomics. Across all studies, none provided complete or consistent reporting of these parameters, with frequent omissions in imaging acquisition and reconstruction details. Methodological and reporting quality remained suboptimal, reflected by median METRICS and CLEAR scores of 52.4% (45-60%) and 62.3% (56-69%), respectively. Reproducibility and quality of radiomics studies would benefit from clear reporting of imaging parameters, consistent documentation of radiomics settings, and control of confounding variables. Additionally, transparency in model validation, preprocessing, and explanation methods would further enhance reproducibility and clinical relevance. Conclusion A focused imaging reproducibility checklist has been developed, and it has been demonstrated that no pancreatic tumour MRI radiomics study reported all necessary imaging parameters for reproducibility. Methodological and reporting quality on broader radiomics components was also poor, highlighting the potential value of such a checklist for improving standardised reporting in radiomics studies. Key points Question There is inconsistent reporting of imaging parameters across MRI protocols used for pancreatic tumours radiomics analysis. Findings The developed MR imaging reporting checklist provides structured guidelines to promote consistent documentation of MR imaging parameters and support reproducible radiomics research. Relevance statement By identifying how key MR imaging acquisition and reconstruction parameters are currently presented in MRI radiomics studies of pancreatic tumours, this study highlights inconsistencies and omissions in reporting, underscoring the need for more transparent reporting and adherence to guidelines to support radiomics reproducibility.

originalAbstract:
Objectives

Radiomics holds potential for personalised treatment, but reproducibility is hindered by inconsistent reporting of imaging parameters and methodological details. This study aims to identify and evaluate key MR imaging parameters to support radiomics reproducibility and to systematically evaluate the quality of published MRI radiomics studies focused on pancreatic tumours.

Materials and methods

The literature search was conducted in the Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science databases. Human studies investigating MRI radiomics in pancreatic tumours were included. An imaging reporting checklist was developed and used to identify and evaluate imaging parameters in eligible studies. The methodological quality score (METRICS) and checklist for evaluation of radiomics research (CLEAR) score were calculated for each study.

Results

Seventy-eight studies, encompassing 241 MRI pulse sequences (143 anatomical and 98 functional), were included. The imaging checklist identified ten core items as key parameters for ensuring reproducible MRI radiomics. Across all studies, none provided complete or consistent reporting of these parameters, with frequent omissions in imaging acquisition and reconstruction details. Methodological and reporting quality remained suboptimal, reflected by median METRICS and CLEAR scores of 52.4% (45-60%) and 62.3% (56-69%), respectively. Reproducibility and quality of radiomics studies would benefit from clear reporting of imaging parameters, consistent documentation of radiomics settings, and control of confounding variables. Additionally, transparency in model validation, preprocessing, and explanation methods would further enhance reproducibility and clinical relevance.

Conclusion

A focused imaging reproducibility checklist has been developed, and it has been demonstrated that no pancreatic tumour MRI radiomics study reported all necessary imaging parameters for reproducibility. Methodological and reporting quality on broader radiomics components was also poor, highlighting the potential value of such a checklist for improving standardised reporting in radiomics studies.

Key points

Question There is inconsistent reporting of imaging parameters across MRI protocols used for pancreatic tumours radiomics analysis. Findings The developed MR imaging reporting checklist provides structured guidelines to promote consistent documentation of MR imaging parameters and support reproducible radiomics research. Relevance statement By identifying how key MR imaging acquisition and reconstruction parameters are currently presented in MRI radiomics studies of pancreatic tumours, this study highlights inconsistencies and omissions in reporting, underscoring the need for more transparent reporting and adherence to guidelines to support radiomics reproducibility.

title: Patient-specific biophysical AI-powered modeling for predicting RFA volumes in HCC.
abstract: Objectives To clinically evaluate a fully automated, artificial intelligence-powered, patient-specific biophysical model for predicting radiofrequency ablation (RFA) volumes in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and to compare its performance with manufacturer-provided ablation estimates. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 96 RFA procedures in 65 HCC patients treated using a single ablation with a cluster needle. Tumors, needle position, and postablation zone were manually segmented on periprocedural computed tomography. Liver parenchyma and vascular structures were automatically extracted using deep learning. A graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated biophysical model simulated heat transfer, vascular heat-sink effects, and tissue necrosis using patient-specific anatomy and procedural data. Correlations between ablation volume manually segmented and clinical or anatomical parameters (ablation time, ablation tip temperature, tumor-capsule distance, vessel proximity, type, and diameter) were assessed. Model-predicted volumes were compared with ground truth and manufacturer estimates using relative volume difference (RVD) and volume similarity. Results Final ablation volumes showed wide variability (7.9-78.8 cm³) and were not correlated with any individual clinical or anatomical parameter (Pearson r - 0.02 to 0.29). Across 94 evaluable cases, simulated and ground-truth volumes were similar (p = 0.165), while manufacturer estimates significantly overestimated ablation volume (p < 0.001). The model achieved a median RVD of 0.39 (interquartile range 0.24-0.57), significantly lower than the manufacturer's algorithm (1.04; 0.64-1.61). Incorporating patient-specific ablation time further improved accuracy. Simulation was fast (0.45 s per second of ablation on GPU). Conclusion A fully automated, patient-specific biophysical model substantially improves RFA ablation volume prediction in HCC compared with manufacturer approximations, supporting its potential role in personalized treatment planning and outcome standardization. Key points Question In patients with hepatocellular carcinoma, can a fully automated, AI-powered, patient-specific biophysical model predict radiofrequency ablation volume more accurately than manufacturer-provided estimates? Findings A fully automated, AI-powered biophysical model integrating patient-specific anatomy and vasculature predicted RFA volume significantly better than manufacturer estimates (median relative volume difference (RVD) 0.39 versus 1.04). Relevance statement Accurate ablation volume prediction could support personalized radiofrequency ablation (RFA) planning, reduce reliance on operator experience, and standardize treatment margins in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), potentially improving local tumor control and reducing recurrence in cirrhotic patients undergoing thermal ablation.

title: Assessment of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease severity using deep learning-based kidney volumetry in CT.
abstract: Objectives Accurate quantification of total kidney volume (TKV) and Mayo imaging classification (MIC) is essential for assessing disease severity in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). This study aimed to develop and validate a deep learning-based method using noncontrast computed tomography (CT) scans to automate TKV measurement and MIC assignment. Materials and methods A retrospective dataset of 60 ADPKD patients was used to train a three-dimensional (3D) UNet model for kidney segmentation and TKV estimation. Kidney axes were calculated using principal component analysis (PCA). The model was tested on consecutive scans from 30 patients (median interval: 3.6 years) and 28 external patient scans. Segmentation accuracy was evaluated using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), and measurement reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). MIC was assigned and compared across timepoints. Results The model achieved high segmentation accuracy (DSC: 0.93 ± 0.04 [mean ± standard deviation] and 0.94 ± 0.03 for consecutive scans; 0.96 ± 0.08 for external validation). Manual and automated TKV measurements were strongly correlated (ICC: 0.94-0.99, p < 0.001), with a mean volume error of 7.61 ± 7.26%. MIC assignment matched in 90-93.3% of cases. Kidney dimensions (length > 16.5 cm, width > 9.5 cm, depth > 8 cm) predicted high-risk MIC classes with positive predictive values > 88%. Longitudinal analysis showed significant increases in TKV and declines in estimated glomerular filtration rate-eGFR (p < 0.001). Conclusion The proposed method enables accurate TKV quantification and MIC classification from noncontrast CT, supporting severity assessment and longitudinal monitoring in ADPKD. Key points Question Can a deep learning method using noncontrast CT accurately automate total kidney volume measurement and Mayo Imaging Classification assignment in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease? Findings In internal and external testing, automated kidney segmentation showed high agreement with reference measurements and correctly assigned Mayo Imaging Classification in most cases with overall accuracy. Relevance statement Automated analysis of noncontrast CT provided reliable kidney volume quantification and disease severity classification, reducing manual workload while enabling longitudinal assessment of disease progression in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.

title: Combining shear wave elastography and ultrasound localization microscopy for liver fibrosis staging in a rat model.
abstract: Objective Accurate staging of liver fibrosis (LF) remains a clinical challenge. This study aimed to quantitatively evaluate the diagnostic value of combining shear wave elastography (SWE) and ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) for LF staging across the full disease spectrum. We sought to integrate liver mechanical properties and microvascular structural parameters to build a multiparametric model for fibrosis staging. Materials and methods LF was induced in Sprague-Dawley rats and histologically staged according to the METAVIR system. A total of 62 rats were included in the final analysis. Both SWE and ULM were performed in each animal. Liver viscoelastic moduli were estimated from SWE data using SW-VEI-Net, a physics-informed neural network-based approach. ULM data were post-processed to reconstruct super-resolution images of the hepatic microvasculature, followed by quantitative analysis to extract microvascular structural parameters. Results Histology revealed fibrosis stages F0 (n = 10), F1 (n = 12), F2 (n = 19), F3 (n = 11), and F4 (n = 10). Compared with the single-modality SWE and ULM models, the multiparametric combined model achieved the highest numerical areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve across the four classification tasks: 0.93 for F0 versus F1-F4, 0.92 for F0-F1 versus F2-F4, 0.90 for F0-F2 versus F3-F4, and 0.89 for F0-F3 versus F4. Conclusion Combining SWE-derived viscoelastic parameters with ULM-derived microvascular features enabled multiparametric characterization of LF in this preclinical rat model. Independent validation in larger animal cohorts and, ultimately, human studies is essential before robust clinical conclusions can be drawn. Key points Question Can combining shear-wave elastography (SWE) and ULM improve the accuracy of LF staging? Findings By integrating viscoelastic and microvascular features, the SWE-ULM combined model achieved the highest numerical AUCs across all four fibrosis classifications in a rat model. Relevance statement The SWE and ULM combined model suggests potential value for LF staging by integrating viscoelastic and microvascular biomarkers, providing a basis for further investigation toward future clinical translation.
